## Medical Debt in Maine: Your Rights, Collection Limits, and Hospital Financial Help (2026)
Source: https://medicaldebtrights.com/states/maine.html

← medicaldebtrights.com home

Medical Debt in Maine: Your Rights, Collection Limits, and Hospital Financial Help (2026)

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Maine residents.

Your Medical Debt Rights in Maine

This page covers pre-bankruptcy medical-debt protections in Maine - the tools that keep medical debt off your credit report, reduce or eliminate your bill at the hospital, and stop aggressive collection before you reach the bankruptcy courthouse.

If you are already being sued or garnished, these protections still apply, but you may need to combine them with FDCPA defenses or bankruptcy filing. See collection limits.

Maine Medical Debt Credit Reporting

Maine enacted medical debt CR protections in 2023-2024 legislative session.

Regardless of state law, the CFPB 2025 Medical Debt Rule (12 CFR Part 1022) bars consumer reporting agencies from including medical debt information on consumer reports used for credit eligibility determinations. This rule applies nationally - including in Maine - and significantly reduces medical debt's effect on credit scores.

The three nationwide CRAs (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) also voluntarily stopped reporting unpaid medical collections under $500 as of 2023, and removed paid medical collections from credit reports starting 2022.

See medical debt credit reporting rules.

Maine Hospital Financial Assistance Policies

Maine Hospital Free Care and Discounted Care program is statutorily mandated.

Every 501(c)(3) nonprofit hospital nationwide must maintain a Financial Assistance Policy (FAP) under 26 U.S.C. Section 501(r). A Maine FAP must:

Establish eligibility criteria based on income, typically tied to federal poverty level (FPL).

Describe the basis for calculating amounts charged to FAP-eligible individuals (cannot exceed "Amounts Generally Billed" to insured patients - AGB).

Describe the FAP application method.

Include a widely publicized plain-language summary.

Be made available free of charge in English and any primary language spoken by 5% of the hospital's service area.

Check the Maine hospital's website, ask at billing, or request a paper FAP - it must be provided. Many Maine patients qualify for substantial or total bill forgiveness under these policies without ever filing for bankruptcy.

See financial assistance applications and charity-care requirements.

501(r) Extraordinary Collection Actions (ECA)

Maine Consumer Credit Code applies.

Under 26 CFR Section 1.501(r)-6, a nonprofit hospital cannot engage in "extraordinary collection actions" (ECAs) against a patient until it has made reasonable efforts to determine whether the patient is FAP-eligible. ECAs include:

Reporting adverse information to credit reporting agencies.

Selling the debt to a collection agency (with limited exceptions).

Deferring or denying medically necessary care because of unpaid bills.

Requiring payment before providing medically necessary care because of prior non-payment.

Filing a civil action.

Placing a lien on property.

Foreclosing on real property.

Attaching or seizing a bank account.

Causing an arrest or body attachment writ.

Garnishing wages.

The "reasonable efforts" window is typically 120 days from the first post-discharge billing statement, with a 240-day application window for the FAP. If an Maine hospital starts ECAs before that window and without proper notification, federal law may require remediation and reporting.

Surprise Billing and the No Surprises Act

The federal No Surprises Act (effective January 1, 2022) bars balance billing for:

Out-of-network emergency services at in-network or out-of-network facilities.

Out-of-network services at in-network facilities (e.g., the anesthesiologist at your in-network hospital).

Out-of-network air ambulance services.

Patients in Maine who receive a balance bill for any of these situations can dispute the bill through federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR). See surprise billing rules.

Maine Medical Debt Collection Limits

ME has robust state protections; apply for state free-care program first.

Federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) rules apply to Maine third-party collectors; many Maine residents also have state-level analogs. If collection conduct includes:

Calls before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m.,

Third-party disclosure of the debt,

Misrepresentation of the amount owed,

Threats of wage garnishment absent a judgment,

...you may have FDCPA claims, which can offset the underlying debt or produce statutory damages up to $1,000 plus attorney fees.

See disputing medical debt.

Insurance Appeals Before Collection

Many Maine medical bills that end up in collections were wrongly denied by insurance. Before accepting a bill as "owed," run the appeal process:

Internal insurance appeal - usually two levels, typically 30-180 days.

External independent review - in Maine, state law plus ERISA or ACA-based external review.

State insurance department complaint.

CMS No Surprises Act complaint for surprise-bill situations.

See insurance appeal process.

Fair Billing Standards for Maine Patients

Under 501(r)(5), nonprofit hospitals cannot charge FAP-eligible patients more than AGB - Amounts Generally Billed, which is calculated as either a look-back method based on commercial insurance and Medicare, or a prospective Medicare-based method. For a Maine FAP-eligible patient, this usually means a 60-80% discount off "chargemaster" rack rates.

Itemized-bill review typically uncovers duplicate charges, incorrect CPT codes, and billed-but-never-performed services. Request the itemized bill in writing; Maine hospitals must provide it.

See fair billing standards.

When Bankruptcy Becomes the Right Tool

After running every pre-bankruptcy lever - FAP application, insurance appeal, itemized-bill review, surprise-billing dispute, CFPB credit-reporting compliance - medical debt that survives is typically unsecured and dischargeable in Chapter 7, or payable at cents-on-the-dollar in Chapter 13.

For Maine debtors who have exhausted pre-bankruptcy tools, see Maine refile timing rules and the 1328(f) discharge screener.

Related Maine Resources

Surprise billing

Insurance appeals

Fair billing

Maryland Medical Debt Collection Limits

MD's state-level protections are among the strongest; pre-bankruptcy FAP is typically successful.

Federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) rules apply to Maryland third-party collectors; many Maryland residents also have state-level analogs. If collection conduct includes:

Calls before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m.,

Third-party disclosure of the debt,

Misrepresentation of the amount owed,

Threats of wage garnishment absent a judgment,

...you may have FDCPA claims, which can offset the underlying debt or produce statutory damages up to $1,000 plus attorney fees.

CMS No Surprises Act complaint for surprise-bill situations.

See fair billing standards.

Out-of-network services at in-network facilities (e.g., the anesthesiologist at your in-network hospital).

Out-of-network air ambulance services.

Patients in Minnesota who receive a balance bill for any of these situations can dispute the bill through federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR). See surprise billing rules.

Minnesota Medical Debt Collection Limits

MN is among the most aggressive state-level protectors; pre-bankruptcy MinnesotaCare and hospital FAP applications typically resolve most medical debt.

Federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) rules apply to Minnesota third-party collectors; many Minnesota residents also have state-level analogs. If collection conduct includes:

Calls before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m.,

Third-party disclosure of the debt,

Misrepresentation of the amount owed,

Threats of wage garnishment absent a judgment,

...you may have FDCPA claims, which can offset the underlying debt or produce statutory damages up to $1,000 plus attorney fees.

See disputing medical debt.

Insurance Appeals Before Collection

Many Minnesota medical bills that end up in collections were wrongly denied by insurance. Before accepting a bill as "owed," run the appeal process:

Internal insurance appeal - usually two levels, typically 30-180 days.

External independent review - in Minnesota, state law plus ERISA or ACA-based external review.

State insurance department complaint.

CMS No Surprises Act complaint for surprise-bill situations.

See insurance appeal process.

Fair Billing Standards for Minnesota Patients

Under 501(r)(5), nonprofit hospitals cannot charge FAP-eligible patients more than AGB - Amounts Generally Billed, which is calculated as either a look-back method based on commercial insurance and Medicare, or a prospective Medicare-based method. For a Minnesota FAP-eligible patient, this usually means a 60-80% discount off "chargemaster" rack rates.

Itemized-bill review typically uncovers duplicate charges, incorrect CPT codes, and billed-but-never-performed services. Request the itemized bill in writing; Minnesota hospitals must provide it.

See fair billing standards.

Minnesota Federal Bankruptcy Data

Medical debt is a leading cause of consumer bankruptcy. The Minnesota consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the downstream scale when pre-bankruptcy protections fail.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 395 consumer bankruptcy cases from Minnesota's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 737999.7%0.3%

Chapter 1316n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

When Bankruptcy Becomes the Right Tool

After running every pre-bankruptcy lever - FAP application, insurance appeal, itemized-bill review, surprise-billing dispute, CFPB credit-reporting compliance - medical debt that survives is typically unsecured and dischargeable in Chapter 7, or payable at cents-on-the-dollar in Chapter 13.

For Minnesota debtors who have exhausted pre-bankruptcy tools, see Minnesota refile timing rules and the 1328(f) discharge screener.

## Medical Debt in Mississippi: Your Rights, Collection Limits, and Hospital Financial Help (2026)
Source: https://medicaldebtrights.com/states/mississippi.html

← medicaldebtrights.com home

Medical Debt in Mississippi: Your Rights, Collection Limits, and Hospital Financial Help (2026)

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Mississippi residents.

Your Medical Debt Rights in Mississippi

This page covers pre-bankruptcy medical-debt protections in Mississippi - the tools that keep medical debt off your credit report, reduce or eliminate your bill at the hospital, and stop aggressive collection before you reach the bankruptcy courthouse.

If you are already being sued or garnished, these protections still apply, but you may need to combine them with FDCPA defenses or bankruptcy filing. See collection limits.

Mississippi Medical Debt Credit Reporting

No state-level CR ban.

Regardless of state law, the CFPB 2025 Medical Debt Rule (12 CFR Part 1022) bars consumer reporting agencies from including medical debt information on consumer reports used for credit eligibility determinations. This rule applies nationally - including in Mississippi - and significantly reduces medical debt's effect on credit scores.

The three nationwide CRAs (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) also voluntarily stopped reporting unpaid medical collections under $500 as of 2023, and removed paid medical collections from credit reports starting 2022.

See medical debt credit reporting rules.

Mississippi Hospital Financial Assistance Policies

Mississippi nonprofit hospitals follow 501(r).

Every 501(c)(3) nonprofit hospital nationwide must maintain a Financial Assistance Policy (FAP) under 26 U.S.C. Section 501(r). A Mississippi FAP must:

Establish eligibility criteria based on income, typically tied to federal poverty level (FPL).

Describe the basis for calculating amounts charged to FAP-eligible individuals (cannot exceed "Amounts Generally Billed" to insured patients - AGB).

Describe the FAP application method.

Include a widely publicized plain-language summary.

Be made available free of charge in English and any primary language spoken by 5% of the hospital's service area.

Check the Mississippi hospital's website, ask at billing, or request a paper FAP - it must be provided. Many Mississippi patients qualify for substantial or total bill forgiveness under these policies without ever filing for bankruptcy.

See financial assistance applications and charity-care requirements.

501(r) Extraordinary Collection Actions (ECA)

501(r)(6) applies.

Under 26 CFR Section 1.501(r)-6, a nonprofit hospital cannot engage in "extraordinary collection actions" (ECAs) against a patient until it has made reasonable efforts to determine whether the patient is FAP-eligible. ECAs include:

Reporting adverse information to credit reporting agencies.

Selling the debt to a collection agency (with limited exceptions).

Deferring or denying medically necessary care because of unpaid bills.

Requiring payment before providing medically necessary care because of prior non-payment.

Filing a civil action.

Placing a lien on property.

Foreclosing on real property.

Attaching or seizing a bank account.

Causing an arrest or body attachment writ.

Garnishing wages.

The "reasonable efforts" window is typically 120 days from the first post-discharge billing statement, with a 240-day application window for the FAP. If an Mississippi hospital starts ECAs before that window and without proper notification, federal law may require remediation and reporting.

Surprise Billing and the No Surprises Act

The federal No Surprises Act (effective January 1, 2022) bars balance billing for:

Out-of-network emergency services at in-network or out-of-network facilities.

Out-of-network services at in-network facilities (e.g., the anesthesiologist at your in-network hospital).

Out-of-network air ambulance services.

Patients in Mississippi who receive a balance bill for any of these situations can dispute the bill through federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR). See surprise billing rules.

Mississippi Medical Debt Collection Limits

MS has high medical debt and chapter 13 dismissal rates; federal 501(r) FAP is primary tool.

Federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) rules apply to Mississippi third-party collectors; many Mississippi residents also have state-level analogs. If collection conduct includes:

Calls before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m.,

Third-party disclosure of the debt,

Misrepresentation of the amount owed,

Threats of wage garnishment absent a judgment,

...you may have FDCPA claims, which can offset the underlying debt or produce statutory damages up to $1,000 plus attorney fees.

See disputing medical debt.

Insurance Appeals Before Collection

Many Mississippi medical bills that end up in collections were wrongly denied by insurance. Before accepting a bill as "owed," run the appeal process:

Internal insurance appeal - usually two levels, typically 30-180 days.

External independent review - in Mississippi, state law plus ERISA or ACA-based external review.

State insurance department complaint.

CMS No Surprises Act complaint for surprise-bill situations.

See insurance appeal process.

Fair Billing Standards for Mississippi Patients

Under 501(r)(5), nonprofit hospitals cannot charge FAP-eligible patients more than AGB - Amounts Generally Billed, which is calculated as either a look-back method based on commercial insurance and Medicare, or a prospective Medicare-based method. For a Mississippi FAP-eligible patient, this usually means a 60-80% discount off "chargemaster" rack rates.

Itemized-bill review typically uncovers duplicate charges, incorrect CPT codes, and billed-but-never-performed services. Request the itemized bill in writing; Mississippi hospitals must provide it.

See fair billing standards.

When Bankruptcy Becomes the Right Tool

After running every pre-bankruptcy lever - FAP application, insurance appeal, itemized-bill review, surprise-billing dispute, CFPB credit-reporting compliance - medical debt that survives is typically unsecured and dischargeable in Chapter 7, or payable at cents-on-the-dollar in Chapter 13.

For Mississippi debtors who have exhausted pre-bankruptcy tools, see Mississippi refile timing rules and the 1328(f) discharge screener.

Nevada Hospital Financial Assistance Policies

Nevada hospital charity-care requirements under NRS Chapter 439B.

Every 501(c)(3) nonprofit hospital nationwide must maintain a Financial Assistance Policy (FAP) under 26 U.S.C. Section 501(r). A Nevada FAP must:

Establish eligibility criteria based on income, typically tied to federal poverty level (FPL).

Describe the basis for calculating amounts charged to FAP-eligible individuals (cannot exceed "Amounts Generally Billed" to insured patients - AGB).

Describe the FAP application method.

Include a widely publicized plain-language summary.

Be made available free of charge in English and any primary language spoken by 5% of the hospital's service area.

Check the Nevada hospital's website, ask at billing, or request a paper FAP - it must be provided. Many Nevada patients qualify for substantial or total bill forgiveness under these policies without ever filing for bankruptcy.

See financial assistance applications and charity-care requirements.

501(r) Extraordinary Collection Actions (ECA)

NV debt collection regulations apply to ECA.

Under 26 CFR Section 1.501(r)-6, a nonprofit hospital cannot engage in "extraordinary collection actions" (ECAs) against a patient until it has made reasonable efforts to determine whether the patient is FAP-eligible. ECAs include:

Reporting adverse information to credit reporting agencies.

Selling the debt to a collection agency (with limited exceptions).

Deferring or denying medically necessary care because of unpaid bills.

Requiring payment before providing medically necessary care because of prior non-payment.

Filing a civil action.

Placing a lien on property.

Foreclosing on real property.

Attaching or seizing a bank account.

Causing an arrest or body attachment writ.

Garnishing wages.

The "reasonable efforts" window is typically 120 days from the first post-discharge billing statement, with a 240-day application window for the FAP. If an Nevada hospital starts ECAs before that window and without proper notification, federal law may require remediation and reporting.

Surprise Billing and the No Surprises Act

The federal No Surprises Act (effective January 1, 2022) bars balance billing for:

Out-of-network emergency services at in-network or out-of-network facilities.

Out-of-network services at in-network facilities (e.g., the anesthesiologist at your in-network hospital).

Out-of-network air ambulance services.

Patients in Nevada who receive a balance bill for any of these situations can dispute the bill through federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR). See surprise billing rules.

Nevada Medical Debt Collection Limits

NV has CR protection; pre-bankruptcy FAP is first step.

Federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) rules apply to Nevada third-party collectors; many Nevada residents also have state-level analogs. If collection conduct includes:

Calls before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m.,

Third-party disclosure of the debt,

Misrepresentation of the amount owed,

Threats of wage garnishment absent a judgment,

...you may have FDCPA claims, which can offset the underlying debt or produce statutory damages up to $1,000 plus attorney fees.

See disputing medical debt.

Insurance Appeals Before Collection

Many Nevada medical bills that end up in collections were wrongly denied by insurance. Before accepting a bill as "owed," run the appeal process:

Internal insurance appeal - usually two levels, typically 30-180 days.

External independent review - in Nevada, state law plus ERISA or ACA-based external review.

State insurance department complaint.

CMS No Surprises Act complaint for surprise-bill situations.

See insurance appeal process.

Fair Billing Standards for Nevada Patients

Under 501(r)(5), nonprofit hospitals cannot charge FAP-eligible patients more than AGB - Amounts Generally Billed, which is calculated as either a look-back method based on commercial insurance and Medicare, or a prospective Medicare-based method. For a Nevada FAP-eligible patient, this usually means a 60-80% discount off "chargemaster" rack rates.

Itemized-bill review typically uncovers duplicate charges, incorrect CPT codes, and billed-but-never-performed services. Request the itemized bill in writing; Nevada hospitals must provide it.

See fair billing standards.

Nevada Federal Bankruptcy Data

Medical debt is a leading cause of consumer bankruptcy. The Nevada consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the downstream scale when pre-bankruptcy protections fail.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 242 consumer bankruptcy cases from Nevada's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 716493.4%5.9%

Chapter 137837.2%62.8%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

When Bankruptcy Becomes the Right Tool

After running every pre-bankruptcy lever - FAP application, insurance appeal, itemized-bill review, surprise-billing dispute, CFPB credit-reporting compliance - medical debt that survives is typically unsecured and dischargeable in Chapter 7, or payable at cents-on-the-dollar in Chapter 13.

For Nevada debtors who have exhausted pre-bankruptcy tools, see Nevada refile timing rules and the 1328(f) discharge screener.

Medical Debt in New Hampshire: Your Rights, Collection Limits, and Hospital Financial Help (2026)

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for New Hampshire residents.

Your Medical Debt Rights in New Hampshire

This page covers pre-bankruptcy medical-debt protections in New Hampshire - the tools that keep medical debt off your credit report, reduce or eliminate your bill at the hospital, and stop aggressive collection before you reach the bankruptcy courthouse.

If you are already being sued or garnished, these protections still apply, but you may need to combine them with FDCPA defenses or bankruptcy filing. See collection limits.

New Hampshire Medical Debt Credit Reporting

No state-level CR ban.

Regardless of state law, the CFPB 2025 Medical Debt Rule (12 CFR Part 1022) bars consumer reporting agencies from including medical debt information on consumer reports used for credit eligibility determinations. This rule applies nationally - including in New Hampshire - and significantly reduces medical debt's effect on credit scores.

The three nationwide CRAs (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) also voluntarily stopped reporting unpaid medical collections under $500 as of 2023, and removed paid medical collections from credit reports starting 2022.

See medical debt credit reporting rules.

New Hampshire Hospital Financial Assistance Policies

NH nonprofit hospitals follow 501(r).

Every 501(c)(3) nonprofit hospital nationwide must maintain a Financial Assistance Policy (FAP) under 26 U.S.C. Section 501(r). A New Hampshire FAP must:

Include a widely publicized plain-language summary.

Out-of-network air ambulance services.

Patients in New Hampshire who receive a balance bill for any of these situations can dispute the bill through federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR). See surprise billing rules.

When Bankruptcy Becomes the Right Tool

After running every pre-bankruptcy lever - FAP application, insurance appeal, itemized-bill review, surprise-billing dispute, CFPB credit-reporting compliance - medical debt that survives is typically unsecured and dischargeable in Chapter 7, or payable at cents-on-the-dollar in Chapter 13.

For New York debtors who have exhausted pre-bankruptcy tools, see New York refile timing rules and the 1328(f) discharge screener.

## Medical Debt in North Carolina: Your Rights, Collection Limits, and Hospital Financial Help (2026)
Source: https://medicaldebtrights.com/states/north-carolina.html

← medicaldebtrights.com home

Medical Debt in North Carolina: Your Rights, Collection Limits, and Hospital Financial Help (2026)

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for North Carolina residents.

Your Medical Debt Rights in North Carolina

This page covers pre-bankruptcy medical-debt protections in North Carolina - the tools that keep medical debt off your credit report, reduce or eliminate your bill at the hospital, and stop aggressive collection before you reach the bankruptcy courthouse.

If you are already being sued or garnished, these protections still apply, but you may need to combine them with FDCPA defenses or bankruptcy filing. See collection limits.

North Carolina Medical Debt Credit Reporting

No state-level CR ban.

Regardless of state law, the CFPB 2025 Medical Debt Rule (12 CFR Part 1022) bars consumer reporting agencies from including medical debt information on consumer reports used for credit eligibility determinations. This rule applies nationally - including in North Carolina - and significantly reduces medical debt's effect on credit scores.

The three nationwide CRAs (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) also voluntarily stopped reporting unpaid medical collections under $500 as of 2023, and removed paid medical collections from credit reports starting 2022.

See medical debt credit reporting rules.

North Carolina Hospital Financial Assistance Policies

North Carolina nonprofit hospitals follow 501(r).

Every 501(c)(3) nonprofit hospital nationwide must maintain a Financial Assistance Policy (FAP) under 26 U.S.C. Section 501(r). A North Carolina FAP must:

Establish eligibility criteria based on income, typically tied to federal poverty level (FPL).

Describe the basis for calculating amounts charged to FAP-eligible individuals (cannot exceed "Amounts Generally Billed" to insured patients - AGB).

Describe the FAP application method.

Include a widely publicized plain-language summary.

Be made available free of charge in English and any primary language spoken by 5% of the hospital's service area.

Check the North Carolina hospital's website, ask at billing, or request a paper FAP - it must be provided. Many North Carolina patients qualify for substantial or total bill forgiveness under these policies without ever filing for bankruptcy.

See financial assistance applications and charity-care requirements.

501(r) Extraordinary Collection Actions (ECA)

501(r)(6) applies.

Under 26 CFR Section 1.501(r)-6, a nonprofit hospital cannot engage in "extraordinary collection actions" (ECAs) against a patient until it has made reasonable efforts to determine whether the patient is FAP-eligible. ECAs include:

Reporting adverse information to credit reporting agencies.

Selling the debt to a collection agency (with limited exceptions).

Deferring or denying medically necessary care because of unpaid bills.

Requiring payment before providing medically necessary care because of prior non-payment.

Filing a civil action.

Placing a lien on property.

Foreclosing on real property.

Attaching or seizing a bank account.

Causing an arrest or body attachment writ.

Garnishing wages.

The "reasonable efforts" window is typically 120 days from the first post-discharge billing statement, with a 240-day application window for the FAP. If an North Carolina hospital starts ECAs before that window and without proper notification, federal law may require remediation and reporting.

Surprise Billing and the No Surprises Act

The federal No Surprises Act (effective January 1, 2022) bars balance billing for:

Out-of-network emergency services at in-network or out-of-network facilities.

Out-of-network services at in-network facilities (e.g., the anesthesiologist at your in-network hospital).

Out-of-network air ambulance services.

Patients in North Carolina who receive a balance bill for any of these situations can dispute the bill through federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR). See surprise billing rules.

North Carolina Medical Debt Collection Limits

Federal framework primary.

Federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) rules apply to North Carolina third-party collectors; many North Carolina residents also have state-level analogs. If collection conduct includes:

Calls before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m.,

Third-party disclosure of the debt,

Misrepresentation of the amount owed,

Threats of wage garnishment absent a judgment,

...you may have FDCPA claims, which can offset the underlying debt or produce statutory damages up to $1,000 plus attorney fees.

See disputing medical debt.

Insurance Appeals Before Collection

Many North Carolina medical bills that end up in collections were wrongly denied by insurance. Before accepting a bill as "owed," run the appeal process:

Internal insurance appeal - usually two levels, typically 30-180 days.

External independent review - in North Carolina, state law plus ERISA or ACA-based external review.

State insurance department complaint.

CMS No Surprises Act complaint for surprise-bill situations.

See insurance appeal process.

Fair Billing Standards for North Carolina Patients

Under 501(r)(5), nonprofit hospitals cannot charge FAP-eligible patients more than AGB - Amounts Generally Billed, which is calculated as either a look-back method based on commercial insurance and Medicare, or a prospective Medicare-based method. For a North Carolina FAP-eligible patient, this usually means a 60-80% discount off "chargemaster" rack rates.

Itemized-bill review typically uncovers duplicate charges, incorrect CPT codes, and billed-but-never-performed services. Request the itemized bill in writing; North Carolina hospitals must provide it.

See fair billing standards.

North Carolina Federal Bankruptcy Data

Medical debt is a leading cause of consumer bankruptcy. The North Carolina consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the downstream scale when pre-bankruptcy protections fail.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 827 consumer bankruptcy cases from North Carolina's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7273n/an/a

Chapter 13554n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

When Bankruptcy Becomes the Right Tool

After running every pre-bankruptcy lever - FAP application, insurance appeal, itemized-bill review, surprise-billing dispute, CFPB credit-reporting compliance - medical debt that survives is typically unsecured and dischargeable in Chapter 7, or payable at cents-on-the-dollar in Chapter 13.

For North Carolina debtors who have exhausted pre-bankruptcy tools, see North Carolina refile timing rules and the 1328(f) discharge screener.

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Ohio residents.

Your Medical Debt Rights in Ohio

This page covers pre-bankruptcy medical-debt protections in Ohio - the tools that keep medical debt off your credit report, reduce or eliminate your bill at the hospital, and stop aggressive collection before you reach the bankruptcy courthouse.

If you are already being sued or garnished, these protections still apply, but you may need to combine them with FDCPA defenses or bankruptcy filing. See collection limits.

Ohio Medical Debt Credit Reporting

No state-level CR ban as of 2026.

Regardless of state law, the CFPB 2025 Medical Debt Rule (12 CFR Part 1022) bars consumer reporting agencies from including medical debt information on consumer reports used for credit eligibility determinations. This rule applies nationally - including in Ohio - and significantly reduces medical debt's effect on credit scores.

Ohio Hospital Care Assurance Program (HCAP) mandates charity care for at-or-below-100%-FPL patients.

Every 501(c)(3) nonprofit hospital nationwide must maintain a Financial Assistance Policy (FAP) under 26 U.S.C. Section 501(r). A Ohio FAP must:

Establish eligibility criteria based on income, typically tied to federal poverty level (FPL).

Describe the basis for calculating amounts charged to FAP-eligible individuals (cannot exceed "Amounts Generally Billed" to insured patients - AGB).

Describe the FAP application method.

Include a widely publicized plain-language summary.

Check the Ohio hospital's website, ask at billing, or request a paper FAP - it must be provided. Many Ohio patients qualify for substantial or total bill forgiveness under these policies without ever filing for bankruptcy.

501(r)(6) and HCAP apply.

Garnishing wages.

Patients in Ohio who receive a balance bill for any of these situations can dispute the bill through federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR). See surprise billing rules.

OH HCAP application is a key pre-bankruptcy step for low-income debtors.

Federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) rules apply to Ohio third-party collectors; many Ohio residents also have state-level analogs. If collection conduct includes:

Calls before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m.,

Third-party disclosure of the debt,

Misrepresentation of the amount owed,

Threats of wage garnishment absent a judgment,

...you may have FDCPA claims, which can offset the underlying debt or produce statutory damages up to $1,000 plus attorney fees.

Many Ohio medical bills that end up in collections were wrongly denied by insurance. Before accepting a bill as "owed," run the appeal process:

Internal insurance appeal - usually two levels, typically 30-180 days.

External independent review - in Ohio, state law plus ERISA or ACA-based external review.

State insurance department complaint.

CMS No Surprises Act complaint for surprise-bill situations.

See insurance appeal process.

Causing an arrest or body attachment writ.

Garnishing wages.

The "reasonable efforts" window is typically 120 days from the first post-discharge billing statement, with a 240-day application window for the FAP. If an Oregon hospital starts ECAs before that window and without proper notification, federal law may require remediation and reporting.

Surprise Billing and the No Surprises Act

The federal No Surprises Act (effective January 1, 2022) bars balance billing for:

Out-of-network emergency services at in-network or out-of-network facilities.

Out-of-network services at in-network facilities (e.g., the anesthesiologist at your in-network hospital).

Out-of-network air ambulance services.

Patients in Oregon who receive a balance bill for any of these situations can dispute the bill through federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR). See surprise billing rules.

Oregon Medical Debt Collection Limits

OR has robust state framework; FAP application typically successful pre-bankruptcy.

Federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) rules apply to Oregon third-party collectors; many Oregon residents also have state-level analogs. If collection conduct includes:

Calls before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m.,

Third-party disclosure of the debt,

Misrepresentation of the amount owed,

Threats of wage garnishment absent a judgment,

...you may have FDCPA claims, which can offset the underlying debt or produce statutory damages up to $1,000 plus attorney fees.

See disputing medical debt.

Insurance Appeals Before Collection

Many Oregon medical bills that end up in collections were wrongly denied by insurance. Before accepting a bill as "owed," run the appeal process:

Internal insurance appeal - usually two levels, typically 30-180 days.

External independent review - in Oregon, state law plus ERISA or ACA-based external review.

State insurance department complaint.

CMS No Surprises Act complaint for surprise-bill situations.

See insurance appeal process.

Fair Billing Standards for Oregon Patients

Under 501(r)(5), nonprofit hospitals cannot charge FAP-eligible patients more than AGB - Amounts Generally Billed, which is calculated as either a look-back method based on commercial insurance and Medicare, or a prospective Medicare-based method. For a Oregon FAP-eligible patient, this usually means a 60-80% discount off "chargemaster" rack rates.

Itemized-bill review typically uncovers duplicate charges, incorrect CPT codes, and billed-but-never-performed services. Request the itemized bill in writing; Oregon hospitals must provide it.

See fair billing standards.

When Bankruptcy Becomes the Right Tool

After running every pre-bankruptcy lever - FAP application, insurance appeal, itemized-bill review, surprise-billing dispute, CFPB credit-reporting compliance - medical debt that survives is typically unsecured and dischargeable in Chapter 7, or payable at cents-on-the-dollar in Chapter 13.

For Oregon debtors who have exhausted pre-bankruptcy tools, see Oregon refile timing rules and the 1328(f) discharge screener.

## Medical Debt in Pennsylvania: Your Rights, Collection Limits, and Hospital Financial Help (2026)
Source: https://medicaldebtrights.com/states/pennsylvania.html

← medicaldebtrights.com home

Medical Debt in Pennsylvania: Your Rights, Collection Limits, and Hospital Financial Help (2026)

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Pennsylvania residents.

Your Medical Debt Rights in Pennsylvania

This page covers pre-bankruptcy medical-debt protections in Pennsylvania - the tools that keep medical debt off your credit report, reduce or eliminate your bill at the hospital, and stop aggressive collection before you reach the bankruptcy courthouse.

If you are already being sued or garnished, these protections still apply, but you may need to combine them with FDCPA defenses or bankruptcy filing. See collection limits.

Pennsylvania Medical Debt Credit Reporting

No state-level CR ban as of 2026.

Regardless of state law, the CFPB 2025 Medical Debt Rule (12 CFR Part 1022) bars consumer reporting agencies from including medical debt information on consumer reports used for credit eligibility determinations. This rule applies nationally - including in Pennsylvania - and significantly reduces medical debt's effect on credit scores.

The three nationwide CRAs (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) also voluntarily stopped reporting unpaid medical collections under $500 as of 2023, and removed paid medical collections from credit reports starting 2022.

See medical debt credit reporting rules.

Pennsylvania Hospital Financial Assistance Policies

Pennsylvania Nonprofit Hospital Community Benefit Act overlays 501(r).

Every 501(c)(3) nonprofit hospital nationwide must maintain a Financial Assistance Policy (FAP) under 26 U.S.C. Section 501(r). A Pennsylvania FAP must:

Establish eligibility criteria based on income, typically tied to federal poverty level (FPL).

Describe the basis for calculating amounts charged to FAP-eligible individuals (cannot exceed "Amounts Generally Billed" to insured patients - AGB).

Describe the FAP application method.

Include a widely publicized plain-language summary.

Be made available free of charge in English and any primary language spoken by 5% of the hospital's service area.

Check the Pennsylvania hospital's website, ask at billing, or request a paper FAP - it must be provided. Many Pennsylvania patients qualify for substantial or total bill forgiveness under these policies without ever filing for bankruptcy.

See financial assistance applications and charity-care requirements.

501(r) Extraordinary Collection Actions (ECA)

501(r)(6) applies.

Under 26 CFR Section 1.501(r)-6, a nonprofit hospital cannot engage in "extraordinary collection actions" (ECAs) against a patient until it has made reasonable efforts to determine whether the patient is FAP-eligible. ECAs include:

Reporting adverse information to credit reporting agencies.

Selling the debt to a collection agency (with limited exceptions).

Deferring or denying medically necessary care because of unpaid bills.

Requiring payment before providing medically necessary care because of prior non-payment.

Filing a civil action.

Placing a lien on property.

Foreclosing on real property.

Attaching or seizing a bank account.

Causing an arrest or body attachment writ.

Garnishing wages.

The "reasonable efforts" window is typically 120 days from the first post-discharge billing statement, with a 240-day application window for the FAP. If an Pennsylvania hospital starts ECAs before that window and without proper notification, federal law may require remediation and reporting.

Surprise Billing and the No Surprises Act

The federal No Surprises Act (effective January 1, 2022) bars balance billing for:

Out-of-network emergency services at in-network or out-of-network facilities.

Out-of-network services at in-network facilities (e.g., the anesthesiologist at your in-network hospital).

Out-of-network air ambulance services.

Patients in Pennsylvania who receive a balance bill for any of these situations can dispute the bill through federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR). See surprise billing rules.

Pennsylvania Medical Debt Collection Limits

PA federal-plus-state-community-benefit framework.

Federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) rules apply to Pennsylvania third-party collectors; many Pennsylvania residents also have state-level analogs. If collection conduct includes:

Calls before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m.,

Third-party disclosure of the debt,

Misrepresentation of the amount owed,

Threats of wage garnishment absent a judgment,

...you may have FDCPA claims, which can offset the underlying debt or produce statutory damages up to $1,000 plus attorney fees.

See disputing medical debt.

Insurance Appeals Before Collection

Many Pennsylvania medical bills that end up in collections were wrongly denied by insurance. Before accepting a bill as "owed," run the appeal process:

Internal insurance appeal - usually two levels, typically 30-180 days.

External independent review - in Pennsylvania, state law plus ERISA or ACA-based external review.

State insurance department complaint.

CMS No Surprises Act complaint for surprise-bill situations.

See insurance appeal process.

Fair Billing Standards for Pennsylvania Patients

Under 501(r)(5), nonprofit hospitals cannot charge FAP-eligible patients more than AGB - Amounts Generally Billed, which is calculated as either a look-back method based on commercial insurance and Medicare, or a prospective Medicare-based method. For a Pennsylvania FAP-eligible patient, this usually means a 60-80% discount off "chargemaster" rack rates.

Itemized-bill review typically uncovers duplicate charges, incorrect CPT codes, and billed-but-never-performed services. Request the itemized bill in writing; Pennsylvania hospitals must provide it.

See fair billing standards.

Pennsylvania Federal Bankruptcy Data

Medical debt is a leading cause of consumer bankruptcy. The Pennsylvania consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the downstream scale when pre-bankruptcy protections fail.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,513 consumer bankruptcy cases from Pennsylvania's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 7415n/an/a

Chapter 131,098n/an/a

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

When Bankruptcy Becomes the Right Tool

After running every pre-bankruptcy lever - FAP application, insurance appeal, itemized-bill review, surprise-billing dispute, CFPB credit-reporting compliance - medical debt that survives is typically unsecured and dischargeable in Chapter 7, or payable at cents-on-the-dollar in Chapter 13.

For Pennsylvania debtors who have exhausted pre-bankruptcy tools, see Pennsylvania refile timing rules and the 1328(f) discharge screener.

Regardless of state law, the CFPB 2025 Medical Debt Rule (12 CFR Part 1022) bars consumer reporting agencies from including medical debt information on consumer reports used for credit eligibility determinations. This rule applies nationally - including in Tennessee - and significantly reduces medical debt's effect on credit scores.

The three nationwide CRAs (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) also voluntarily stopped reporting unpaid medical collections under $500 as of 2023, and removed paid medical collections from credit reports starting 2022.

See medical debt credit reporting rules.

Tennessee Hospital Financial Assistance Policies

Tennessee nonprofit hospitals follow 501(r).

Every 501(c)(3) nonprofit hospital nationwide must maintain a Financial Assistance Policy (FAP) under 26 U.S.C. Section 501(r). A Tennessee FAP must:

Establish eligibility criteria based on income, typically tied to federal poverty level (FPL).

Describe the basis for calculating amounts charged to FAP-eligible individuals (cannot exceed "Amounts Generally Billed" to insured patients - AGB).

Describe the FAP application method.

Include a widely publicized plain-language summary.

Be made available free of charge in English and any primary language spoken by 5% of the hospital's service area.

Check the Tennessee hospital's website, ask at billing, or request a paper FAP - it must be provided. Many Tennessee patients qualify for substantial or total bill forgiveness under these policies without ever filing for bankruptcy.

See financial assistance applications and charity-care requirements.

501(r) Extraordinary Collection Actions (ECA)

501(r)(6) applies.

Under 26 CFR Section 1.501(r)-6, a nonprofit hospital cannot engage in "extraordinary collection actions" (ECAs) against a patient until it has made reasonable efforts to determine whether the patient is FAP-eligible. ECAs include:

Reporting adverse information to credit reporting agencies.

Selling the debt to a collection agency (with limited exceptions).

Deferring or denying medically necessary care because of unpaid bills.

Requiring payment before providing medically necessary care because of prior non-payment.

Filing a civil action.

Placing a lien on property.

Foreclosing on real property.

Attaching or seizing a bank account.

Causing an arrest or body attachment writ.

Garnishing wages.

The "reasonable efforts" window is typically 120 days from the first post-discharge billing statement, with a 240-day application window for the FAP. If an Tennessee hospital starts ECAs before that window and without proper notification, federal law may require remediation and reporting.

Surprise Billing and the No Surprises Act

The federal No Surprises Act (effective January 1, 2022) bars balance billing for:

Out-of-network emergency services at in-network or out-of-network facilities.

Out-of-network services at in-network facilities (e.g., the anesthesiologist at your in-network hospital).

Out-of-network air ambulance services.

Patients in Tennessee who receive a balance bill for any of these situations can dispute the bill through federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR). See surprise billing rules.

Tennessee Medical Debt Collection Limits

TN chapter 13 dismissal rates are high; pre-bankruptcy FAP application is critical.

Federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) rules apply to Tennessee third-party collectors; many Tennessee residents also have state-level analogs. If collection conduct includes:

Calls before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m.,

Third-party disclosure of the debt,

Misrepresentation of the amount owed,

Threats of wage garnishment absent a judgment,

...you may have FDCPA claims, which can offset the underlying debt or produce statutory damages up to $1,000 plus attorney fees.

See disputing medical debt.

Insurance Appeals Before Collection

Many Tennessee medical bills that end up in collections were wrongly denied by insurance. Before accepting a bill as "owed," run the appeal process:

Internal insurance appeal - usually two levels, typically 30-180 days.

External independent review - in Tennessee, state law plus ERISA or ACA-based external review.

State insurance department complaint.

CMS No Surprises Act complaint for surprise-bill situations.

See insurance appeal process.

Fair Billing Standards for Tennessee Patients

Under 501(r)(5), nonprofit hospitals cannot charge FAP-eligible patients more than AGB - Amounts Generally Billed, which is calculated as either a look-back method based on commercial insurance and Medicare, or a prospective Medicare-based method. For a Tennessee FAP-eligible patient, this usually means a 60-80% discount off "chargemaster" rack rates.

Itemized-bill review typically uncovers duplicate charges, incorrect CPT codes, and billed-but-never-performed services. Request the itemized bill in writing; Tennessee hospitals must provide it.

See fair billing standards.

Tennessee Federal Bankruptcy Data

Medical debt is a leading cause of consumer bankruptcy. The Tennessee consumer bankruptcy volume below shows the downstream scale when pre-bankruptcy protections fail.

Numbers below come from the Federal Judicial Center Integrated Database covering 1,840 consumer bankruptcy cases from Tennessee's federal bankruptcy courts.

ChapterCases FiledDischarge RateDismissal Rate

Chapter 758995.5%4.5%

Chapter 131,25117.3%82.7%

Rates computed on resolved cases only. Source: FJC Integrated Database.

When Bankruptcy Becomes the Right Tool

After running every pre-bankruptcy lever - FAP application, insurance appeal, itemized-bill review, surprise-billing dispute, CFPB credit-reporting compliance - medical debt that survives is typically unsecured and dischargeable in Chapter 7, or payable at cents-on-the-dollar in Chapter 13.

For Tennessee debtors who have exhausted pre-bankruptcy tools, see Tennessee refile timing rules and the 1328(f) discharge screener.

Medical Debt in Texas: Your Rights, Collection Limits, and Hospital Financial Help (2026)

Your Medical Debt Rights in Texas

This page covers pre-bankruptcy medical-debt protections in Texas - the tools that keep medical debt off your credit report, reduce or eliminate your bill at the hospital, and stop aggressive collection before you reach the bankruptcy courthouse.

Out-of-network air ambulance services.

Patients in Texas who receive a balance bill for any of these situations can dispute the bill through federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR). See surprise billing rules.

Texas Medical Debt Collection Limits

TX has strong homestead protection; medical debt rarely threatens home, but wage garnishment concerns are largely preempted by Texas law.

Federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) rules apply to Texas third-party collectors; many Texas residents also have state-level analogs. If collection conduct includes:

Calls before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m.,

Third-party disclosure of the debt,

Threats of wage garnishment absent a judgment,

...you may have FDCPA claims, which can offset the underlying debt or produce statutory damages up to $1,000 plus attorney fees.

State insurance department complaint.

CMS No Surprises Act complaint for surprise-bill situations.

See insurance appeal process.

When Bankruptcy Becomes the Right Tool

After running every pre-bankruptcy lever - FAP application, insurance appeal, itemized-bill review, surprise-billing dispute, CFPB credit-reporting compliance - medical debt that survives is typically unsecured and dischargeable in Chapter 7, or payable at cents-on-the-dollar in Chapter 13.

For Virginia debtors who have exhausted pre-bankruptcy tools, see Virginia refile timing rules and the 1328(f) discharge screener.

## Medical Debt in Washington: Your Rights, Collection Limits, and Hospital Financial Help (2026)
Source: https://medicaldebtrights.com/states/washington.html

← medicaldebtrights.com home

Medical Debt in Washington: Your Rights, Collection Limits, and Hospital Financial Help (2026)

State-specific rules, federal court data, and practical guidance for Washington residents.

Your Medical Debt Rights in Washington

This page covers pre-bankruptcy medical-debt protections in Washington - the tools that keep medical debt off your credit report, reduce or eliminate your bill at the hospital, and stop aggressive collection before you reach the bankruptcy courthouse.

If you are already being sued or garnished, these protections still apply, but you may need to combine them with FDCPA defenses or bankruptcy filing. See collection limits.

Washington Medical Debt Credit Reporting

Washington state has medical debt CR protections.

Regardless of state law, the CFPB 2025 Medical Debt Rule (12 CFR Part 1022) bars consumer reporting agencies from including medical debt information on consumer reports used for credit eligibility determinations. This rule applies nationally - including in Washington - and significantly reduces medical debt's effect on credit scores.

The three nationwide CRAs (Equifax, Experian, TransUnion) also voluntarily stopped reporting unpaid medical collections under $500 as of 2023, and removed paid medical collections from credit reports starting 2022.

See medical debt credit reporting rules.

Washington Hospital Financial Assistance Policies

Washington's Charity Care Act (RCW 70.170) requires all hospitals (not just nonprofits) to provide charity care; 2022 amendments expanded the income threshold.

Every 501(c)(3) nonprofit hospital nationwide must maintain a Financial Assistance Policy (FAP) under 26 U.S.C. Section 501(r). A Washington FAP must:

Establish eligibility criteria based on income, typically tied to federal poverty level (FPL).

Describe the basis for calculating amounts charged to FAP-eligible individuals (cannot exceed "Amounts Generally Billed" to insured patients - AGB).

Describe the FAP application method.

Include a widely publicized plain-language summary.

Be made available free of charge in English and any primary language spoken by 5% of the hospital's service area.

Check the Washington hospital's website, ask at billing, or request a paper FAP - it must be provided. Many Washington patients qualify for substantial or total bill forgiveness under these policies without ever filing for bankruptcy.

See financial assistance applications and charity-care requirements.

501(r) Extraordinary Collection Actions (ECA)

Washington Consumer Protection Act applies.

Under 26 CFR Section 1.501(r)-6, a nonprofit hospital cannot engage in "extraordinary collection actions" (ECAs) against a patient until it has made reasonable efforts to determine whether the patient is FAP-eligible. ECAs include:

Reporting adverse information to credit reporting agencies.

Selling the debt to a collection agency (with limited exceptions).

Deferring or denying medically necessary care because of unpaid bills.

Requiring payment before providing medically necessary care because of prior non-payment.

Filing a civil action.

Placing a lien on property.

Foreclosing on real property.

Attaching or seizing a bank account.

Causing an arrest or body attachment writ.

Garnishing wages.

The "reasonable efforts" window is typically 120 days from the first post-discharge billing statement, with a 240-day application window for the FAP. If an Washington hospital starts ECAs before that window and without proper notification, federal law may require remediation and reporting.

Surprise Billing and the No Surprises Act

The federal No Surprises Act (effective January 1, 2022) bars balance billing for:

Out-of-network emergency services at in-network or out-of-network facilities.

Out-of-network services at in-network facilities (e.g., the anesthesiologist at your in-network hospital).

Out-of-network air ambulance services.

Patients in Washington who receive a balance bill for any of these situations can dispute the bill through federal Independent Dispute Resolution (IDR). See surprise billing rules.

Washington Medical Debt Collection Limits

WA has the strongest state-level hospital charity-care mandate in the country. Apply first.

Federal Fair Debt Collection Practices Act (FDCPA) rules apply to Washington third-party collectors; many Washington residents also have state-level analogs. If collection conduct includes:

Calls before 8 a.m. or after 9 p.m.,

Third-party disclosure of the debt,

Misrepresentation of the amount owed,

Threats of wage garnishment absent a judgment,

...you may have FDCPA claims, which can offset the underlying debt or produce statutory damages up to $1,000 plus attorney fees.

See disputing medical debt.

Insurance Appeals Before Collection

Many Washington medical bills that end up in collections were wrongly denied by insurance. Before accepting a bill as "owed," run the appeal process:

Internal insurance appeal - usually two levels, typically 30-180 days.

External independent review - in Washington, state law plus ERISA or ACA-based external review.

State insurance department complaint.

CMS No Surprises Act complaint for surprise-bill situations.

See insurance appeal process.

Fair Billing Standards for Washington Patients

Under 501(r)(5), nonprofit hospitals cannot charge FAP-eligible patients more than AGB - Amounts Generally Billed, which is calculated as either a look-back method based on commercial insurance and Medicare, or a prospective Medicare-based method. For a Washington FAP-eligible patient, this usually means a 60-80% discount off "chargemaster" rack rates.

Itemized-bill review typically uncovers duplicate charges, incorrect CPT codes, and billed-but-never-performed services. Request the itemized bill in writing; Washington hospitals must provide it.

See fair billing standards.

When Bankruptcy Becomes the Right Tool

After running every pre-bankruptcy lever - FAP application, insurance appeal, itemized-bill review, surprise-billing dispute, CFPB credit-reporting compliance - medical debt that survives is typically unsecured and dischargeable in Chapter 7, or payable at cents-on-the-dollar in Chapter 13.

For Washington debtors who have exhausted pre-bankruptcy tools, see Washington refile timing rules and the 1328(f) discharge screener.
